name: Z-Wave
label: Z-Wave
notes: Z-Wave frames (ITU-T G.9959), decoded by OnAir's receiver through the onair-rx handler; the row has no decoder of its own, so only a handler runs it. One job reads every channel of one region inside its band: start it with a band of 2 MHz (the handler takes 2 MHz of IQ; EU's three channels, 868.42, 868.40 and 869.85 MHz, fit around 869.13 MHz) and it exits at start when no region has a channel inside the band. Each event is a frame: `home_id` (8 hex digits, the network), `src` and `dst` (node ids as integers; 255 is the broadcast; a multicast has no `dst`), `frame_type` (`singlecast`, `multicast`, `ack`, `routed`), `rate_bps` (9600, 40000 or 100000), `freq_hz`, `secured` (an S0 or S2 payload, which stays encrypted) and `len`. OnAir's packet carries the data rate and not the channel, so `freq_hz` is inferred from the region and the rate and is null where the band holds two channels of one rate (Japan, Korea). Nothing is decrypted; the MPDUs (a byte for the data rate, then the frame, link type 148) go to a packet capture. Ranges and bands: the regions (EU, US, ANZ, HK, IN, RU, CN, IL, JP, KR) and so the ranges 865 to 870 and 908 to 927 MHz are the channel tables of the ITU-T G.9959 regional frequencies as OnAir carries them; the channels at 9.6, 40 and 100 kbit/s fit a 100 kHz band. Listing bar: measured on the build host (12 cores) through a scratch node's release build, 30 s of the generated capture looping on a file source and fed in real time; the job skipped no input, onair-rx used 0.03 of a core and the node 0.08 of a core (load average 4.4 to 3.8, with another build running).
